blocks.title: FLOWER – A Fascinating Organ of Angiosperm-Introduction
blocks.text:
• To a biologist, flowers are morphological and embryological marvels and the sites of sexual reproduction.

• Much before the actual flower is seen on a plant, the decision that the plant is going to flower has taken place.
    • Several hormonal and structural changes are initiated which lead to the differentiation and further development of the floral primordium.
    • Inflorescences are formed which bear the floral buds and then the flowers. In the flower the male and female reproductive structures, the androecium and the gynoecium differentiate and develop .

blocks.title: Core Concept - FLOWER - A Fascinating Organ of Angiosperms
blocks.text:
STRUCTURE OF FLOWER :-

• Flower is a modified shoot.
    • Unisexual Male flower - Staminate
• Unisexual Female flower - Pistillate

    • Both Male and Female flowers are present on the same plant - Monoecious, e.g. Cucurbits, Coconut
    • Male and Female flowers present on separate plants - Dioecious e.g. Papaya, Date palm

blocks.title: PYQ2
blocks.question:
The female reproductive part of a flower is-

(1) Androecium

(2) Calyx

(3) Corolla

(4) Gynoecium
blocks.answer:
Option - 4

The female reproductive part of a flower is the gynoecium, also known as the pistil. The gynoecium is the innermost whorl of a flower and is made up of pistils. The gynoecium produces ovules, which develop into seeds after fertilization, and the gynoecium itself turns into a fruit.

blocks.question:
Flowers are unisexual in :-

(1) Onion               (2) Pea

(3) Cucumber        (4) China rose
blocks.answer:
Answer = 3

  • Cucumber
Cucumber plants have monoecious flowers, meaning both male and female flowers appear on the same plant. The male flowers grow first, followed by the female flowers.
  • Onion, pea, and china rose
These plants have bisexual flowers, which means they contain both androecium and gynoecium.

blocks.title: Core Concepts : The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule)
blocks.text:
Female reproductive whorl - Gynoecium :-

• Monocarpellary
    • Multicarpellary

(a) A dissected flower of Hibiscus showing pistil
(b) Multicarpellary, syncarpous gynoecium of Papaver ;
(c) A multicarpellary, apocarpous gynoecium of Michelia ;
(d) A diagrammatic view of typical anatropous ovule

• Ovary with one ovule - wheat, paddy, mango • Ovary with many ovules – papaya, watermelon, orchid

Structure of Ovule :-

• Typical anatropous ovule.
    • Funicle - stalk of ovule
    • Hilum - the junction between ovule and funicle
    • Integuments - one or two protective envelopes
    • Nucellus - main part of ovule,cells- abundant reserve food
    • Micropyle - small opening
    • Chalaza - representing the basal part of the ovule.
Located in the nucellus is the embryo sac or female gametophyte. An ovule generally has a single embryo sac formed from a megaspore.

blocks.title: Megasporogenesis
blocks.text:
Megasporogenesis :-   megaspore mother cell —> meiosis division → megaspores.

• Ovules differentiate a single megaspore mother cell (MMC) in the micropylar region of the nucellus.

blocks.title: Development of Female Gametophyte
blocks.text:
Development of female gametophyte:

  • One megaspore mother cell—->4 megaspores formed
  • Out of 4 megaspores one megaspore remains functional while the other three degenerate.
  • Functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte (embryo sac).
• This method of embryo sac formation from a single megaspore is termed  monosporic development

blocks.title: PYQ 1
blocks.question:
Given below are two statements (for angiosperm plants) :-

Statement-I : A mature male gametophyte possess two male gametes.

Statement-II : A mature female gametophyte is 7-celled and 8 nucleated in   typical angiosperms.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

(1) Both Statement-I and II are correct.

(2) Statement-I is correct but statement-II is incorrect.

(3) Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct.

(4) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are incorrect.
blocks.answer:
Answer (1)

Mature male gametophyte in angiosperms is a three-celled structure i.e., the 3-celled germinated pollen grain. The terminal poistion is occupied by cytoplasm and nucleus of tube cell and two male gametes remain in back side of tube nucleus. In 40% of angiosperms, pollen is released at the 3-celled stage while in other 60% in the 2-celled immature stage.
So, the correct answer is 'Three celled'.
options: (1) Both Statement-I and II are correct.
(2) Statement-I is correct but statement-II is incorrect.
(3) Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct.
(4) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are incorrect.

blocks.title: PYQ 2
blocks.question:
Which is the most common type of embryo sac in angiosperms ?

(1) Tetrasporic with one mitotic stage of divisions

(2) Monosporic with three sequential mitotic divisions

(3) Monosporic with two sequential mitotic divisions

(4) Bisporic with two sequential mitotic divisions
blocks.answer:
Answer (2)

In the monosporic type, a single megaspore undergoes three rounds of mitosis to form a seven-celled, eight-nucleate structure. This type of embryo sac is also known as the Polygonum type, named after the plant Polygonum.
options: (1) Tetrasporic with one mitotic stage of divisions
(2) Monosporic with three sequential mitotic divisions
(3) Monosporic with two sequential mitotic divisions
(4) Bisporic with two sequential mitotic divisions

blocks.title: Core Concepts: Pollination
blocks.text:
POLLINATION:-

Transfer of pollen grains from anther to the stigma.

  • In Commelina, Viola and Oxalis are two different types of flowers. Cleistogamous and Chasmogamous flowers.
  • Cleistogamous flowers are invariably autogamous and assured seed set even in the absence of pollinators.

blocks.title: Self Pollinated Flowers and 𝘾𝙤𝙢𝙢𝙚𝙡𝙞𝙣𝙖 Plant
blocks.caption: Diagram

blocks.title: Cross Pollination
blocks.text:
• Both water and wind pollinated flowers are not very colourfull and do not produce nectar.
        • Majority of insect-pollinated flowers are large, colourful, fragrant and rich in nectar.
        • When the flowers are small, a number of flowers are clustered into an inflorescence to make them conspicuous.
        • Often flowers of animal pollinated plants are specifically adapted for a particular species of animal
        • Fly and beetle pollinating flower :- Foul odour
        • To sustain animal visits, the flowers have to provide rewards to the animals. Nectar and pollen grains are the usual floral rewards.
        • In some species floral rewards are in providing safe places to lay eggs. example-tallest flower of Amorphophallus ,species of moth and the plant Yucca.

• Pollen/nectar robber :- Many insects may consume pollen or the nectar without bringing about pollination.
    • Floral rewards provided to pollinator :-  Edible pollen, nectar and safe place for laying eggs.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing pollination with fertilization: Misunderstanding that pollination is the transfer of pollen, while fertilization is the fusion of gametes.
  • Overlooking types of pollination: Failing to differentiate between self-pollination (autogamy) and cross-pollination (allogamy).
  • Misrepresenting agents of pollination: Assuming only insects are pollinators, ignoring wind, water, birds, bats, and other animals
  • Confusing self-compatibility with self-pollination: Believing all self-pollinating plants are self-compatible, ignoring mechanisms like self-incompatibility.
  • Misunderstanding pollination syndromes: Attributing traits like color or scent incorrectly to specific pollinators.

Q.2 Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Cleistogamous flowers are invariably autogamous

Statement II: Cleistogamy is disadvantageous as there is no chance for cross-pollination.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

(1) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect

(2) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect

(3) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

(4) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
blocks.answer:
Answer (4)

Cleistogamous flowers do not open at all. In such flowers, the anthers and stigma lie close to each other. When anthers dehisce in the flower buds, pollen grains come in contact with the stigma to affect pollination. Thus, Cleistogamous flowers are in variably autogenous as there is no chance of cross-pollen landing on the stigma.

blocks.title: Pollen -Pistil interaction
blocks.text:
Pollen pistil interaction :-

• All events from pollen deposition on stigma until pollen tube enters in ovule.

• Biochemical of pollen and pistil are involved.
    • Biochemical interaction.
    • Dynamic and continuous process.
    • Pollen recognition followed by acceptance and rejection of pollen grain by pistil.

blocks.title: Core Concepts: Fertilizations
blocks.text:
Fertilization :-

(A) Germination of pollen grain :-

• Pollen grain germinates on the stigma to produce a pollen tube.
    • Pollen tube grows through the tissues of stigma and style to reach the ovule.
    • Generative cell divides mitotically to form 2 male gametes
    • Both male gametes are non-motile.
(B) Entry of pollen tube into the ovule and embryo sac :-

• Generally entry of pollen tube in ovule through the micropyle.
    • The filiform apparatus present at the micropylar part of synergids guides the entry of the pollen tube.
    • Pollen tube enters in embryo sac through degenerating synergid.

• Enlarged view of an egg apparatus showing entry of pollen tube into a synergid

• Discharge of male gametes into synergid and movements of the male gametes, one into the egg and other into the central cell

(C) Double Fertilization :-

• Pollen tube releases the two male gametes inside the cytoplasm of degenerating synergid of embryo sac.

• Double fertilization is unique event to flowering plants.
    • Double fertilization : Syngamy + Triple fusion
Syngamy :-
Male gamete + female gamete $\rightarrow$ Zygote ( 2 n )

Triple fusion :-
Male gamete + Two polar nuclei $\rightarrow$ Primary endosperm nucleus ( 3 n )

(central cell becomes PEC after triple fusion)

blocks.title: PYQ 1
blocks.question:
Double fertilization involves: -

(1)Fertilization of the egg by two male gametes

(2) Fertilization of two eggs in the same embryosac by two sperms brought by           one pollen tube

(3) Fertilization of the egg and the central cell by two sperms (male gametes) brought by different pollen tubes

(4) Fertilization of the egg and the central cell by two sperms (male gametes) brought by the same pollen tube.
blocks.answer:
Answer(4)

Double fertilization is a unique feature of angiosperms (flowering plants). It involves:

  • One male gamete fusing with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote (2n).
  • Another male gamete fusing with the central cell (which has two polar nuclei) to form a triploid endosperm (3n).
Both male gametes are delivered by a single pollen tube.
options: (1)Fertilization of the egg by two male gametes
(2) Fertilization of two eggs in the same embryosac by two sperms brought by           one pollen tube
(3) Fertilization of the egg and the central cell by two sperms
(4) Fertilization of the egg and the central cell by two sperms

  • (c) Male sex organs in angiosperms are called stamens, present in flowers.      • Correct: Stamens are the male reproductive organs of flowering plants (angiosperms). They typically consist of a filament and an anther, which produces pollen grains.

blocks.title: PYQ 3
blocks.question:
What is the fate of the male gametes discharged in the synergid?

(1) One fuses with the egg, other(s) degenerate(s) in the synergid.

(2) All fuse with the egg.

(3) One fuses with the egg, other(s) fuse(s) with synergid nucleus.

(4) One fuses with the egg and other fuses with central cell nuclei.
blocks.answer:
Answer (4)

The fate of the male gametes discharged in the synergid is that one fuses with the egg and the other fuses with the central cell nuclei.

In flowering plants, two male gametes are released in the synergids. One of the gametes fuses with the egg, and the other fuses with the secondary or definitive nucleus in the central cell.
options: (1) One fuses with the egg, other
(3) One fuses with the egg, other
(4) One fuses with the egg and other fuses with central cell nuclei.

blocks.title: Core Concept Post-Fertilization-Events
blocks.text:
Following double fertilisation, events of endosperm and embryo development, maturation of ovule(s) into seed(s) and ovary into fruit, are collectively termed postfertilization events.

Post - Fertilization : Structures and Events :-

(A) Development of Endosperm :-

• Endosperm development precedes embryo development.

PEC $\xrightarrow[\text { divisions }]{\text { Nuclear }}$ Multinudeate structure $\xrightarrow[\text { formation }]{\text { Cell wall }}$ Endosperm

• The number of free nuclei formed before cellularisation varies greatly.
    • Coconut water : Nuclear endosperm.
    • White kernel of coconut : Cellular endosperm.

blocks.title: Embryo Development
blocks.text:
(B) Development of Embryo :-

• The process of development of embryo from zygote is called embryogenesis or embryogeny.
    • Embryo develops at the micropylar end of the embryosac.
    • Most zygotes divide only after certain amount of endosperm is formed.
    • Early stages of embryo development are similar in both monocot & dicot.
    • The zygote gives rise to the proembryo and subsequently to the globular, heart-shaped and mature embryo.

• A typical embryo of angiosperm consists of one or two cotyledon(s) and embryonal axis with a radicle and a plumule.
    • Portion of embryonal axis above the level of attachment of cotyledon(s) is known as epicotyl.
    • Portion of embryonal axis below the level of attachment of cotyledon(s) is known as hypocotyl.

blocks.title: PYQ 1
blocks.question:
Given below are two statements; one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason(R) :-

Assertion (A) : In angiosperm plants, nuclear endosperm is most common.

Reason (R) : When formation of endosperm occurs due to free nuclear division, is called cellular endosperm.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

(1) If (A) & (R) both are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

(2) (A) is correct but (R) is incorrect.

(3) (A) is not correct but (R) is correct.

(4) If (A) & (R) both are correct and (R) is the correct explanation
blocks.answer:
Answer (2)

  • Assertion (A) is correct: In the most common type of endosperm development, the PEN undergoes successive nuclear divisions to give rise to free nuclei. This stage of endosperm development is known as free-nuclear endosperm.
  • Reason (R) is incorrect: The PEN undergoes successive nuclear divisions to give rise to free nuclei. This stage of endosperm development is called free- nuclear endosperm. Subsequently, cell wall formation occurs and the endosperm becomes cellular.
options: (A) and the other is labelled as Reason
(A) : In angiosperm plants, nuclear endosperm is most common.

blocks.title: PYQ 3
blocks.question:
The hilum is a scar on the :-

(1) Fruit, where it was attached to pedicel

(2) Fruit, where style was present

(3) Seed, where micropyle was present

(4) Seed, where funicle was attached
blocks.answer:
Ans- 4

The hilum is a scar on the seed, where the funicle was attached. The hilum is a whitish oval scar on the concave side of the seed.

The funiculus is a stalk of the ovule. The hilum is the point where the ovule's body attaches to the funiculus. After fertilization, the hilum appears as a scar on the mature seed.

A small pore called the micropyle is located near the hilum. The germinating seed absorbs water through the micropyle, and it also allows respiratory gases to diffuse.
options: (1) Fruit, where it was attached to pedicel

(1) Antipodals, synergids, and primary endosperm nucleus

(2) Synergids, Zygote, and Primary endosperm nucleus

In a fertilized embryo sac the haploid, diploid and triploid structures are synergid, zygote and primary endosperm respectively.

blocks.title: Core Concepts : Angiospermic Seed
blocks.text:
ANGIOSPERM SEED :-
    • Fertilized ovule
    • Final product of sexual reproduction.
    • Seeds are formed inside fruits.
    • Seed typically consists of the seed coat(s), cotyledon(s), and an embryonal axis with a radicle and a plumule.
    • Non-albuminous/ex-albuminous seed e.g. Pea, Groundnut.
    • Albuminous seeds e.g. Wheat, Maize, Barley, Castor.
    • Residual, persistent nucellus is the perisperm : Black pepper, Beet.
    • Integument of ovule hardens and forms seed coat.
    • Micropyle provides entry of water and oxygen during seed germination.

As the seed matures, its water content is reduced, and it becomes relatively dry ( 10 to 15 % moisture).
    • After fertilization, ovule develops into seed and ovary develops into fruit simultaneously.
    • Ovary wall develops thick wall, pericarp.
    • Fleshy fruit : Guava, orange & mango
    • Dry fruit : Ground nut & mustard
    • True fruit develops only from ovary.
False fruit: Fruit is developed from other parts of the flower along with the ovary. In strawberries, apples, and cashews, the thalamus also contributes to fruit formation.
    • Parthenocarpic fruit : Fruits develop without fertilization eg. banana.

blocks.title: Type of Seed
blocks.text:
• The angiosperm seeds are classified into two categories based on the presence or absence of endosperm in seeds
(a) Non Endospermic or Ex-albuminous seed or Non albuminous seeds :- seeds do not have an endosperm at maturity, so they are called non-endospermic.

Examples : Capsella and most dicotyledons (gram, pea, bean, ground nut). But in castor, seeds are endospermic.

(b) Endospermic or Albuminous seeds :- endosperm not completely used up during embryo development ,Endosperm present , food is stored in endosperm.

Examples : Most of monocot seeds (wheat, rice, coconut, barley and maize etc). But in orchid ,seeds are non-endospermic.

blocks.title: PYQ1
blocks.question:
Read the following four statements (A-D):-

(A) Pericarp is fleshy in mango, orange and guava.

(B) Apple and pear are example of false fruits.

(C) In dicot seed, the root cap is enclosed in an undifferentiated sheath called coleorhiza.

(D) In the dicot seed, the zygote gives rise to the proembryo and subsequently to the

globular, heart-shaped and mature embryo.

How many of the above statements are correct?

(1) One                     (2) Three

(3) Two                     (4) four
blocks.answer:
Answer (2)

(A) Pericarp is fleshy in mango, orange, and guava.

  • This statement is correct. The pericarp (fruit wall) in these fruits is fleshy.
(B) Apple and pear are examples of false fruits.

  • This statement is correct. Apple and pear are false fruits because the fleshy part is derived from the receptacle (flower base), not just the ovary.
(C) In dicot seed, the root cap is enclosed in an undifferentiated sheath called coleorhiza.

  • This statement is incorrect. The coleorhiza is found in monocot seeds, not dicot seeds. In dicot seeds, the root cap is not enclosed in a coleorhiza.
(D) In the dicot seed, the zygote gives rise to the proembryo and subsequently to the globular, heart-shaped, and mature embryo.

  • This statement is correct. The development of the embryo in dicots progresses through stages: proembryo → globular → heart-shaped → mature embryo.

blocks.question:
Persistent nucellus in the seed is known as :-

(4) Tegmen
blocks.answer:
Answer (2)

  • Hilum is the scar on a seed that marks the point of attachment to the ovary wall.
  • Tegmen is the inner layer of the seed coat.

blocks.answer:

blocks.title: FLOWER – A Fascinating Organ of Angiosperm-Introduction
blocks.text:
• To a biologist, flowers are morphological and embryological marvels and the sites of sexual reproduction.

• Much before the actual flower is seen on a plant, the decision that the plant is going to flower has taken place.
    • Several hormonal and structural changes are initiated which lead to the differentiation and further development of the floral primordium.
    • Inflorescences are formed which bear the floral buds and then the flowers. In the flower the male and female reproductive structures, the androecium and the gynoecium differentiate and develop .

blocks.title: Core Concepts: Male Reproductive Whorl
blocks.text: Male reproductive whorl

blocks.title: Core Concepts : The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule)
blocks.text:
Female reproductive whorl - Gynoecium :-

• Monocarpellary
    • Multicarpellary

(a) A dissected flower of Hibiscus showing pistil
(b) Multicarpellary, syncarpous gynoecium of Papaver ;
(c) A multicarpellary, apocarpous gynoecium of Michelia ;
(d) A diagrammatic view of typical anatropous ovule

• Ovary with one ovule - wheat, paddy, mango • Ovary with many ovules – papaya, watermelon, orchid

Structure of Ovule :-

• Typical anatropous ovule.
    • Funicle - stalk of ovule
    • Hilum - the junction between ovule and funicle
    • Integuments - one or two protective envelopes
    • Nucellus - main part of ovule,cells- abundant reserve food
    • Micropyle - small opening
    • Chalaza - representing the basal part of the ovule.
Located in the nucellus is the embryo sac or female gametophyte. An ovule generally has a single embryo sac formed from a megaspore.

blocks.title: Development of Female Gametophyte
blocks.text:
Development of female gametophyte:

  • One megaspore mother cell—->4 megaspores formed
  • Out of 4 megaspores one megaspore remains functional while the other three degenerate.
  • Functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte (embryo sac).
• This method of embryo sac formation from a single megaspore is termed  monosporic development

blocks.title: Cross Pollination
blocks.text:
• Both water and wind pollinated flowers are not very colourfull and do not produce nectar.
        • Majority of insect-pollinated flowers are large, colourful, fragrant and rich in nectar.
        • When the flowers are small, a number of flowers are clustered into an inflorescence to make them conspicuous.
        • Often flowers of animal pollinated plants are specifically adapted for a particular species of animal
        • Fly and beetle pollinating flower :- Foul odour
        • To sustain animal visits, the flowers have to provide rewards to the animals. Nectar and pollen grains are the usual floral rewards.
        • In some species floral rewards are in providing safe places to lay eggs. example-tallest flower of Amorphophallus ,species of moth and the plant Yucca.

• Pollen/nectar robber :- Many insects may consume pollen or the nectar without bringing about pollination.
    • Floral rewards provided to pollinator :-  Edible pollen, nectar and safe place for laying eggs.

blocks.title: Core Concepts: Fertilizations
blocks.text:
Fertilization :-

(A) Germination of pollen grain :-

• Pollen grain germinates on the stigma to produce a pollen tube.
    • Pollen tube grows through the tissues of stigma and style to reach the ovule.
    • Generative cell divides mitotically to form 2 male gametes
    • Both male gametes are non-motile.
(B) Entry of pollen tube into the ovule and embryo sac :-

• Generally entry of pollen tube in ovule through the micropyle.
    • The filiform apparatus present at the micropylar part of synergids guides the entry of the pollen tube.
    • Pollen tube enters in embryo sac through degenerating synergid.

• Enlarged view of an egg apparatus showing entry of pollen tube into a synergid

• Discharge of male gametes into synergid and movements of the male gametes, one into the egg and other into the central cell

(C) Double Fertilization :-

• Pollen tube releases the two male gametes inside the cytoplasm of degenerating synergid of embryo sac.

• Double fertilization is unique event to flowering plants.
    • Double fertilization : Syngamy + Triple fusion
Syngamy :-
Male gamete + female gamete $\rightarrow$ Zygote ( 2 n )

Triple fusion :-
Male gamete + Two polar nuclei $\rightarrow$ Primary endosperm nucleus ( 3 n )

(central cell becomes PEC after triple fusion)

blocks.title: Core Concept Post-Fertilization-Events
blocks.text:
Following double fertilisation, events of endosperm and embryo development, maturation of ovule(s) into seed(s) and ovary into fruit, are collectively termed postfertilization events.

Post - Fertilization : Structures and Events :-

(A) Development of Endosperm :-

• Endosperm development precedes embryo development.

PEC $\xrightarrow[\text { divisions }]{\text { Nuclear }}$ Multinudeate structure $\xrightarrow[\text { formation }]{\text { Cell wall }}$ Endosperm

• The number of free nuclei formed before cellularisation varies greatly.
    • Coconut water : Nuclear endosperm.
    • White kernel of coconut : Cellular endosperm.

blocks.title: Embryo Development
blocks.text:
(B) Development of Embryo :-

• The process of development of embryo from zygote is called embryogenesis or embryogeny.
    • Embryo develops at the micropylar end of the embryosac.
    • Most zygotes divide only after certain amount of endosperm is formed.
    • Early stages of embryo development are similar in both monocot & dicot.
    • The zygote gives rise to the proembryo and subsequently to the globular, heart-shaped and mature embryo.

• A typical embryo of angiosperm consists of one or two cotyledon(s) and embryonal axis with a radicle and a plumule.
    • Portion of embryonal axis above the level of attachment of cotyledon(s) is known as epicotyl.
    • Portion of embryonal axis below the level of attachment of cotyledon(s) is known as hypocotyl.

blocks.title: Core Concepts : Angiospermic Seed
blocks.text:
ANGIOSPERM SEED :-
    • Fertilized ovule
    • Final product of sexual reproduction.
    • Seeds are formed inside fruits.
    • Seed typically consists of the seed coat(s), cotyledon(s), and an embryonal axis with a radicle and a plumule.
    • Non-albuminous/ex-albuminous seed e.g. Pea, Groundnut.
    • Albuminous seeds e.g. Wheat, Maize, Barley, Castor.
    • Residual, persistent nucellus is the perisperm : Black pepper, Beet.
    • Integument of ovule hardens and forms seed coat.
    • Micropyle provides entry of water and oxygen during seed germination.

As the seed matures, its water content is reduced, and it becomes relatively dry ( 10 to 15 % moisture).
    • After fertilization, ovule develops into seed and ovary develops into fruit simultaneously.
    • Ovary wall develops thick wall, pericarp.
    • Fleshy fruit : Guava, orange & mango
    • Dry fruit : Ground nut & mustard
    • True fruit develops only from ovary.
False fruit: Fruit is developed from other parts of the flower along with the ovary. In strawberries, apples, and cashews, the thalamus also contributes to fruit formation.
    • Parthenocarpic fruit : Fruits develop without fertilization eg. banana.

blocks.title: Type of Seed
blocks.text:
• The angiosperm seeds are classified into two categories based on the presence or absence of endosperm in seeds
(a) Non Endospermic or Ex-albuminous seed or Non albuminous seeds :- seeds do not have an endosperm at maturity, so they are called non-endospermic.

Examples : Capsella and most dicotyledons (gram, pea, bean, ground nut). But in castor, seeds are endospermic.

(b) Endospermic or Albuminous seeds :- endosperm not completely used up during embryo development ,Endosperm present , food is stored in endosperm.

Examples : Most of monocot seeds (wheat, rice, coconut, barley and maize etc). But in orchid ,seeds are non-endospermic.

    • Polyembryony: Occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing pollination with fertilization: Misunderstanding that pollination is the transfer of pollen, while fertilization is the fusion of gametes.
  • Overlooking types of pollination: Failing to differentiate between self-pollination (autogamy) and cross-pollination (allogamy).
  • Misrepresenting agents of pollination: Assuming only insects are pollinators, ignoring wind, water, birds, bats, and other animals
  • Confusing self-compatibility with self-pollination: Believing all self-pollinating plants are self-compatible, ignoring mechanisms like self-incompatibility.
  • Misunderstanding pollination syndromes: Attributing traits like color or scent incorrectly to specific pollinators.

STRUCTURE OF FLOWER :-
